title: Edge Decisioning: Concurrency & Fanout Discovery
summary: Discovery focused on meeting Crownline's hard p95 latency target for an edge decisioning product that fans out to many microservices. Discussed hosted vs dedicated vs private tradeoffs, token/sec benchmarking, streaming vs non-streaming, autoscaling, and a plan for a short pilot benchmark.
action_items: Liam Chen: send high-level Dedicated vs Private pricing + example cost per million tokens (due 2029-05-17)
Priya Nair: draft benchmark plan (A100/H100) with sample prompt set and infra recipe (due 2029-05-20)
Aisha Rahman: share 48h traffic traces and current p95 measurements for their internal policy engine (due 2029-05-16)
next_steps: Schedule 2-hour pilot kickoff to run token/sec and latency+concurrency benchmarks (tentative 2029-05-22)
Redwood to provide secure upload link for trace data and a short non-prod deployment manifest
Customer to review SOC2 and encryption docs (link shared in chat)
transcript:
Meeting header: 2029-05-14 16:00 UTC | Duration 54m | Recording id ff-20290514-crownline-01
Attendees: Liam (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Marcus (Crownline Head of Platform), Aisha (ML Infra Lead), Tomás (CTO)

[00:00:00] Liam: hey everyone thanks for joining today, appreciate you squeezing this in. quick intros?
[00:00:07] Marcus: yeah Marcus here — platform, we own the decisioning infra that sits at the edge, we basically accept events from our gateway and then fanout to multiple downstream microservices.
[00:00:17] Aisha: hi I'm Aisha, I lead ML infra, mainly worry about latency, cold starts, and privacy for the customer signals.
[00:00:22] Tomás: Tomás, CTO, i'm mostly here for high-level constraints and to make sure we can meet our SLA.
[00:00:27] Liam: great. priya and I will run through how Redwood handles p95 and throughput and then get into benchmarks. quick context question — what's your target p95 for the decision path?
[00:00:36] Marcus: objective is 200ms p95 from event in to final action for the main fast-path. we do have a slower path for complex scoring that can be 1s plus, but the fast path can't exceed 200.
[00:00:45] Priya: 200ms p95 is tight for an LLM-based step, can you walk me through where you plan to run the model — is this on-prem near the gateway or in cloud?
[00:00:54] Marcus: we're exploring both. prefer hosted for speed-to-market but worried about multi-tenant noisy neighbors. Dedicated or private options sound interesting.
[00:01:03] Aisha: also the fanout is a multiplier — we typically fan out to 3 downstream scoring services after the model, so the model step budget is ~80-100ms to keep overall path within 200ms.
[00:01:12] Liam: good detail — that explains the requirement. a couple of things to raise up front: continuous streaming with early token outputs can shave latency, and prefix/KV cache reuse is big if you have repeated context. but at 80-100ms budget, you'll likely need either an optimized quantized model on dedicated hardware or a private on-prem setup.
[00:01:28] Tomás: when you say streaming, do you mean server-sent chunks or something like a streaming websocket? we do websockets to the gateway.
[00:01:33] Priya: yeah streaming response via websocket is what Redwood supports; crucial part is how frequently we flush tokens and the transport overhead — we usually benchmark token/sec and p95 for the first token and for full completion.
[00:01:44] Marcus: first token p95 is the real metric for us. completion time is less relevant for the fast-path because we stop after top-1.
[00:01:50] Aisha: we also have a 99th percentile cost concern — if a few long requests blow up our cost we need throttles that degrade gracefully.
[00:01:57] Liam: got it. so for measurement plan we'll separate two things: first-token p95 (cold and warm), and sustained tokens/sec for steady-state concurrency.
[00:02:06] Priya: couple of clarifying Qs — how many concurrent requests at peak do you expect?
[00:02:11] Marcus: current peak is ~1,200 rps across their global edge points, but each request fans out — after routing we expect about 400 concurrent model requests at the central inference layer during peaks.
[00:02:23] Tomás: and we want room to scale 2x without a hard rearchitect.
[00:02:26] Priya: cool. that maps to batching and autoscaling strategies. for p95 targets at 80-100ms we'd probably recommend a model variant that's latency-optimized — e.g., 7B/13B quantized on H100 with low-latency kernels, or dedicated A100 pools if you're going hosted and need predictability.
[00:02:41] Aisha: curious: how much variance do you see with shared hosted vs dedicated for first-token p95?
[00:02:46] Liam: in our experience shared hosted has more jitter; p95 might be 1.5-2x worse under noisy workloads compared to dedicated. dedicated pools reduce tail variance and give you predictable throughput. private on-prem gives you the tightest tail but has the longest lead time to set up.
[00:02:59] Marcus: ok can you give numbers — like, if we target 80ms first token, what hardware and config do we need?
[00:03:05] Priya: rough rule of thumb: on H100 with optimized kernels and quantization you can get first-token p95 for a trimmed 13B to ~40-70ms depending on sequence length and model architecture. On A100 it's maybe ~60-120ms. These are warm numbers. Cold start adds more.
[00:03:21] Tomás: warm numbers sound promising. cold starts are a worry though — we can't afford cold-starts to exceed 300ms often.
[00:03:28] Priya: we recommend pre-warmed standby instances for the fast path, and Redwood's smart routing can fallback to smaller model variants if latency spikes. autoscaling with a warm-buffer is common.
[00:03:38] Marcus: you mentioned quantization and kernels — will Redwood handle tuning for us or we need to bring a tuned model?
[00:03:44] Liam: Redwood does the quantization and kernel selection as part of onboarding for Dedicated and Private customers. For hosted we have curated model variants and recommended quant profiles. We'll produce a verified performance profile per model.
[00:03:55] Aisha: security question — for Private we'd need KMS integration and audit logs. we also need SSO and SAML for admin console.
[00:04:03] Liam: absolutely; Private includes customer-managed KMS, HSM options, audit logs, and SAML/SSO. We'll share SOC2 + encryption docs after the call.
[00:04:11] Tomás: what about data residency — some of our EU traffic must stay in EU regions.
[00:04:15] Liam: we support region pinning and can route requests to EU-hosted capacity or stand up Dedicated in your chosen region.
[00:04:21] Marcus: ok let's talk benchmarks — what would Redwood need from us to run a realistic test?
[00:04:26] Priya: ideal: 48h of request traces (timestamps, seq lengths, prompt types) and a sample prompt set representing the fast path. Also your typical concurrency pattern and allowable test windows. We can provide a small harness that replays traces against hosted/dedicated/private configs.
[00:04:39] Aisha: we can anonymize traces, yes. we'll need a secure upload link.
[00:04:42] Liam: we'll send a secure S3 presigned link and a minimal manifest. Priya will draft the benchmark plan.
[00:04:48] Tomás: who owns the infra during the pilot if we pick Private? like will Redwood help with on-prem deployment?
[00:04:53] Liam: Redwood's Private package includes deployment support — we have an on-prem installer and SE support for the first 2 sprints. For Dedicated we'll manage the infra.
[00:05:00] Marcus: cost — ballpark numbers for dedicated pools to serve 400 concurrent requests with low tail?
[00:05:05] Liam: i'll follow up with a cost model, but directionally Dedicated monthly commit for a medium pool could be comparable to a few hundred thousand dollars per month depending on hours and redundancy. We'll present cost/per-token and a few sizing options.
[00:05:16] Aisha: ok please include a delta for H100 vs A100 in that cost model.
[00:05:19] Liam: noted.
[00:05:21] Priya: technical: one more concern — our fanout means ephemeral parallelism after the model. Do you support per-token throttles and backpressure to the gateway?
[00:05:30] Liam: yes, Redwood's routing supports request shaping and token-level rate limiting; you can set per-route SLOs and automatic fallbacks that will skew traffic to smaller models or to cached responses when tails heat up.
[00:05:42] Marcus: great. can you do a quick sketch of the benchmark phases?
[00:05:45] Priya: sure — phase 1: baseline single-request latency (first-token p95 warm/cold) across model variants on A100/H100; phase 2: concurrency ramp (0->2x expected) measuring tokens/sec and p95 at increments; phase 3: fanout simulation with downstream latencies to evaluate end-to-end 200ms p95; phase 4: failover/fallback validation — simulate noisy neighbor and verify graceful degradation. We'll log token-level latencies and KV cache hit rates.
[00:06:13] Tomás: timeline?
[00:06:15] Priya: if we get traces by 2029-05-16 we can run an initial hosted and dedicated baseline by 2029-05-22. Private on-prem baseline depends on lead time — typically 4-6 weeks for air-gapped installs.
[00:06:26] Aisha: sounds reasonable. question about model size: are you recommending smaller decoder-only models or something like Llama-3 style?
[00:06:33] Priya: architecture matters — some 13B decoders with optimized attention can be faster than a poorly optimized 7B. We'll recommend specific family/variant per accuracy/latency tradeoff. We'll also provide a regression harness to compare quality across rollouts.
[00:06:47] Marcus: one operational ask — we need traceable rollout controls for canaries and quick rollback if quality regresses.
[00:06:52] Liam: Redwood Console supports canary rollouts, percentage-based traffic splits, and immediate fallback to previous model. We'll add a doc link in the follow-up.
[00:06:59] Tomás: any red flags we should watch for in the benchmark?
[00:07:03] Priya: watch sequence length distributions — tail long sequences blow up tokens/sec. Also watch KV cache effectiveness; if your prompts don't repeat prefixes, caching won't help. And network egress between regions can add ms.
[00:07:16] Marcus: we'll include sequence length percentiles in the trace.
[00:07:19] Aisha: last question — for streaming, what bucket sizes do you flush at to balance transport vs latency?
[00:07:25] Priya: typical flush every 16-32 tokens for low-latency settings, but for very short completions we flush at first-token immediately. There's some tuning. We'll test flush granularity in our phase 1 runs.
[00:07:36] Liam: ok i'll recap: Redwood sends secure upload link and pricing deck; Priya to send benchmark plan; Crownline to share traces by 5/16; target pilot kickoff week of 5/22.
[00:07:47] Marcus: yep that matches.
[00:07:49] Tomás: please include H100/A100 comparisons and the warm-buffer autoscale recipe.
[00:07:54] Liam: will do. Anything else?
[00:07:56] Aisha: maybe include notes about audit log format — we ingest logs into our SIEM.
[00:08:01] Liam: noted, we'll share sample audit log format.
[00:08:05] Marcus: thanks everyone.
[00:08:07] Liam: thanks — end of recorded segment, relaxed chatter after call.

Note: transcript contains natural hesitations and minor transcription errors typical of automated transcripts (e.g., some proper nouns spelled phonetically). Links referenced in chat: pricing deck (link), SOC2 & encryption docs (link), benchmark harness repo (link).
